doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

title: RCA Christmas album and the Beatles record
summary: Promoting the Christmas record, then the Beatles record that ended RCA's support.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: okay. Aside from then having like personal troubles in my life, I’m like losing my voice, in between all of this stuff that’s going on. But the record gets made. And then we go to promote it, and Sebesky, we’re going to promote it at the Blue Note and Sebesky writes new chart for the band, and Ron Fair says, “well we’ve got to record Avalon, this is all new, we need to do that as well as” — well we were doing the Christmas in the middle of the show. We go in the studio and it’s January and we record all this, because the band’s hot. Great. So and there’s another $100,000. Okay. It’s not coming out of my pocket.
Don’t say anything because this might—

I’m swinging. So you know, but now you ran into all the like rock & roll publicists and all that, and the review guys are saying, “oh Pizzarelli has big budget records” and he’s this and he’s that. And like well hey, what am I supposed to do? I’m going to make a small group record? I’m having the time of my life working with the best people, and making good records. And then, there’s the fateful Beatle record. I made a Beat Meets the Beatles record, and Sebesky writes the charts and it’s killing and there’s strings and we had all this great stuff and all the rock & roll people at RCA said no more, no more Pizzarelli. They didn’t get it. I thought, the idea was we can take our style, use Beatles music to attract people who wouldn’t listen to us. And it was a blatant attempt to sell records because that’s how you make a living, I always thought, you try to sell records, which reviewers always say, “he’s trying to sell records.”
